# Mon Nov 09 - Randomized blocks and nested effects

Today we consider some more examples of fixed and random effects for two categorical explanatory variables.

- [Ch13.4 Randomized blocks](https://davidcschneider.github.io/StatisticalScience/LNotes/Pt4/Ch13_4.pdf)

- [Ch13.6 Heirachical ANOVA (Nested effects)](https://davidcschneider.github.io/StatisticalScience/LNotes/Pt4/Ch13_6.pdf)

We will also discuss calculating adjusted sum of squares to determine whether individual terms in models are significant. See [here](#adj-SS).

## Randomized blocks

The flour beetle _Tribolium casteneum_ was a model lab organism for establishing the
basic facts and principles of quantitative genetics, including inbreeding and response to
selection. Once the whole genome was sequenced, Tribolium was used in
immunohistochemistry, in situ hybridization, gene sequencing for characterization of
microRNAs, and gene editing.

_Tribolium_ is a major pest of stored grain. Economic losses consist of reduced weight and
product quality, difficulties in baking, reduced marketability of infested products, and an
accompanying unpleasant smell. Pest numbers are reduced by sieving or by adding inert
dusts that cause death by dessication.

This study illustrates a randomized block design, which has a fixed and a random factor.
The randomized block is an example of statistical control, in which the effects of one
variable (the random factor) are removed in order to arrive at a better analysis of the fixed
factor. This analysis is a more sensitive test because it removes some of the noise in the
data before testing. The paired t-test is a special case of the randomized block, in which
the fixed factor has just two categories.

**Verbal model** Does weight of flour beetle Tribolium vary among genotype, after controlling for
differences among experiments ? Genotype bb is a mutant strain, for which the expected
weights are least for the homozygote bb and greatest for the heterozygote +b.
The analysis removes the effects of blocks. This results in a more sensitive test of
whether weight varies among genotypes.

## Load the data and assess assumptions

```{r}
beetle.data = read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ahurford/biol-4605-data/refs/heads/main/data/tribolium.csv")
beetle.data
```

These data are a bit ambiguous so I will do some renaming to avoid errors:

```{r,message=FALSE}
require(dplyr)
beetle.data = beetle.data%>%mutate(genotype = case_when(Gtype == 1 ~ "++",
                                          Gtype == 2 ~ "+b",
                                          Gtype == 3 ~ "bb"))%>%rename(weight=Wt)
beetle.data$block=as.factor(beetle.data$block)
beetle.data
```

```{r,message=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(beetle.data, aes(x = factor(genotype), y = weight)) +
  # 1. Add the box plot layer
  geom_boxplot(
    outlier.shape = NA,       # CRITICAL: Prevents duplicate plotting of outliers
    fill = "grey95",          # Light fill to keep it as a background summary
    color = c("maroon","darkgray","lightblue")         # Muted border color
  ) +
  geom_line(aes(group = block, color = block), alpha = 0.7)+
  # 2. Add the strip plot (jittered points) layer
  geom_jitter(aes(color=block),
    position = position_jitter(width = 0, height = 0), # Controls data spreading - we need not spreading for this paired plot to work.
    size = 5,                 # Modify point size
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Genotype",
    y = "weight (grams)",
    title = "Visualize the data (randomized block)"
  )+theme_minimal()
```

## Write the model and execute the analysis

\[
M = \beta_0 + \beta_B B + \beta_G G + \epsilon
\]
or
\[
Y_{ijk} = \mu + B_j + \alpha_i + \epsilon_{ij}
\]


```{r,message=FALSE}
require(lme4)
require(lmerTest)
beetle.model = lmer(weight~(1|block)+genotype, data=beetle.data)
summary(beetle.model)
anova(beetle.model)
```

```{r,message=FALSE}
beetle.model2 = aov(weight~Error(block)+genotype, data=beetle.data)
summary(beetle.model2)
```

## Hierachical ANOVA (nested effects)

### Data

Two measurements made on the left wings of 4 mosquitos in each of 3 cages.
This is a nested design. We cannot match flies across cages.
At a lower level, we cannot match wing measurements across flies.


### Nested models

Two-way ANOVA has an interaction term. Testing starts with this term.

In randomized blocks, the interaction term is present logically, but assumed to be zero if
blocks are homogeneous.

Hierarchical ANOVA differs from crossed designs. The interaction term $\mbox{Fly} \times \mbox{Cage}$
cannot be estimated. It is folded into a new term: $\mbox{Fly(Cage)} = \mbox{Cage} + \mbox{Fly} \times \mbox{Cage}$.

In this example, we have no information to match a fly in Cage I (Fly A, B, C, D) to a fly in Cage II (Fly
E, F, G, H). Fly is nested within cage. Consider this diagrammatically.

```{r}
wing.data = read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ahurford/biol-4605-data/refs/heads/main/data/fly-cage.csv")
wing.data
```

## Execute the analysis

```{r}
fly.model = aov(length ~ cage + Error(cage/fly), wing.data)
summary(fly.model)
```
